label: Thirty Tigers
description: Old News keeps The Steel Woods' heavy riffing intact while sharpening the band's storytelling on songs about addiction, mortality and hard-won faith, recorded not long before Jason Cope's death. It is a strong second landmark showing the band's growth as writers within the genre. Recommended as a companion to the debut.
lineage: A continuation of The Steel Woods' branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage with deepening Americana songwriting, still oriented toward mainstream rock/Americana audiences rather than the Core.

label: Tricki-Woo Records
description: Sisters Rebecca and Megan Lovell push their roots-rock sound toward heavier blues-rock on Venom & Faith, built around slide guitar, stomping rhythms and reworked blues and gospel standards alongside originals. It shows a related mainstream continuation of Southern guitar-rock filtered through blues rather than boogie-rock radio. Recommended for the slide-guitar, blues-rock branch of the lane.
lineage: A blues-rock-leaning branch off V28's Southern guitar-rock lineage (via the Allman Brothers' slide-guitar tradition specifically), heading toward the contemporary blues-rock circuit rather than the punk-adjacent Core.

label: Tricki-Woo Records
description: Blood Harmony won the 2024 Grammy for Best Contemporary Blues Album, pairing the Lovell sisters' close harmonies and slide-guitar riffing with the band's most polished, arena-scaled production yet. It represents the commercial high point of the blues-rock wing of Southern rock's mainstream continuation. A strong recent landmark for the lane.
lineage: Continues Larkin Poe's branch off V28's Southern slide-guitar lineage into Grammy-recognized mainstream blues-rock, distinct from both the boogie-rock (Blackberry Smoke) and jam-band (Allman Betts) wings of the same lane.

label: Mercury Nashville
description: Musgraves' major-label debut is wry, plainspoken country songwriting aimed at small-town Texas life, weed jokes and quiet rebellion under a traditional pedal-steel-and-fiddle Nashville sound. It landed as a critics' favorite inside the mainstream country machine, opening the door for a run of pop crossover that followed. A clean entry point for how a country insider can read as an indie-friendly songwriter.
lineage: Grows out of mainstream Nashville songwriting (X1) filtered through Cosmic American Music's plainspoken lineage (V21); leads forward into Musgraves' own pop-crossover arc rather than toward the Core scene.

label: MCA Nashville
description: Musgraves' pivot record folds disco shimmer and vocoder into her pedal-steel country base, trading jokes for a wide-open, in-love glow. It became the template for 'country as mode' crossover success that Cowboy Carter and Post Malone's country turn later followed at pop scale. Essential for hearing how far the genre's edges can stretch while keeping a steel guitar in the mix.
lineage: Splits from the mainstream-Nashville/Cosmic American Music line (X1/V21) toward adult-pop production; the branch runs onward into 2020s pop-country crossovers like Cowboy Carter and F-1 Trillion rather than into the indie-twang Core.

label: Sub Pop
description: A masked, mysterious persona singing lonesome-cowboy ballads over reverb-heavy Telecaret twang and shoegaze-tinged production, closer to Chris Isaak or Roy Orbison than to Nashville radio. Released on indie stalwart Sub Pop rather than a country label, it is the clearest 'indie artist adopts country iconography' landmark of the 2010s. Good starting point for the queer/theatrical branch of the country-turn trend.
lineage: Descends from mainstream country's outlaw-and-crooner imagery via the indie label system (X1) rather than the twang scene proper; the branch runs on through his own major-label albums (Bronco, Stampede) rather than into Core indie twang.

label: Columbia
description: A major-label-scaled follow-up to Pony, trading some of the debut's mystery for widescreen, string-and-pedal-steel Americana and guest-heavy production. It shows the country-turn persona graduating from cult indie status to a bigger pop stage. Representative of how far the Peck project moved from Sub Pop-scale intimacy toward mainstream country crossover.
lineage: Continues Peck's outlaw-persona branch off mainstream country/X1 into major-label pop-country territory; does not feed back into the indie-twang Core.

album: If My Wife New I'd Be Dead
label: CMATBaby/AWAL
description: The Irish pop singer's debut reframes breakup pain as broad, funny, hooky country-pop, pairing pedal steel with big choruses and self-deprecating one-liners. It is the field-guide entry point for CMAT's country turn: a pop songwriter reaching for Nashville signifiers to sharpen emotional whiplash rather than to join the genre outright. Good for listeners who want Dolly Parton wit filtered through 2020s indie-pop production.
lineage: Splits off mainstream country's confessional songwriting mode (X1) through an Irish indie-pop lens; leads onward through CMAT's own catalog rather than into the twang Core.
key_tracks: I Wanna Be a Cowboy, Baby!

label: CMATBaby/AWAL
description: CMAT's second album widens the scope with orchestral flourishes and even bigger country-pop hooks while keeping the same sardonic, oversharing lyric style about family and disastrous romance. It confirmed her as the UK/Ireland's most visible pop-to-country crossover artist. A strong second landmark showing the persona maturing beyond the debut's novelty framing.
lineage: Continues CMAT's branch off mainstream country songwriting (X1) into arena-pop scale; stays in the pop-country lane rather than joining indie twang.

label: CMATBaby/AWAL
description: CMAT's third album leans further into arena-scaled country-pop with sardonic, sometimes political lyrics about Ireland and modern life, as Josh Terry described it as "witty, sardonic pop-country with arena-filling choruses." It cements CMAT as the field-guide artist for this lane's contemporary edge. Landed on year-end best-of lists as one of 2025's most acclaimed pop-country records.
lineage: Continues CMAT's pop-country branch off X1/mainstream country songwriting; the newest data point in the trend, feeding forward rather than back toward the Core.
key_tracks: Take a Sexy Picture of Me

label: Parkwood Entertainment/Columbia
description: A pop superstar's sprawling, star-studded reckoning with country music's Black roots, mixing traditional pedal steel and banjo arrangements with hip-hop and R&B production and guest turns from Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson and Linda Martell. It is the highest-profile landmark of pop artists claiming country as a mode, explicitly framed as a genre-history statement rather than a genre-immersion record. Essential listening for understanding the scale this trend reached by the mid-2020s.
lineage: Splits off mainstream Nashville country and its history of erasing Black country artists (X1) via a pop superstar's lens; the branch runs forward into pop and country radio rather than into indie twang.

album: The Land Is Inhospitable and So Are We
label: Dead Oceans
description: Mitski strips back her usual maximalism for a hushed, string-laden record that Wikipedia describes as Americana, country and folk-inflected, closer to spare orchestral pop than any Nashville sound. Josh Terry called it "uniformly gorgeous and powerful even when subdued," praising how she reins in her pop impulses. It is a borderline but real example of an indie-pop artist reaching toward country/Americana textures rather than a country record proper.
lineage: Splits off Americana and country folk's spare, string-backed songwriting (adjacent to X1/V21 territory) through Mitski's indie-rock background; the branch stays within her own art-pop catalog rather than feeding the Core scene.

label: Mercury/Republic
description: The hip-hop/pop star's full turn to country, built on duets with Tim McGraw, Chris Stapleton, Billy Strings and Sierra Ferrell over pedal steel and Telecaret twang, marking his rebrand as a Nashville-adjacent artist. It is the biggest commercial 'pop artist becomes country artist' event of the mid-2020s, running parallel to Cowboy Carter. A useful landmark for the sheer scale of mainstream pop's country pivot.
lineage: Splits off mainstream Nashville duet culture and outlaw-country signifiers (X1) via a pop/hip-hop star's rebrand; leads forward into country radio rather than into the indie twang Core.

label: Reprise
description: A spare, dulcimer-and-piano confessional record that became the defining Laurel Canyon singer-songwriter statement, all raw diary-entry lyrics and an unmistakable soaring voice. It set the emotional-honesty template that Jackson Browne, Linda Ronstadt and generations of confessional songwriters after her worked from. The clearest entry point into the LA scene this lane covers.
lineage: Grows out of the folk-revival songwriting that also fed Cosmic American Music (V21) and Dylan/The Band's roots turn (V22); its confessional-songwriter line runs forward into mainstream singer-songwriter pop rather than into the twang-scene Core.

label: Asylum
description: Mitchell's commercial peak folds jazz-tinged arrangements and studio-band polish (with members of the Crusaders) into her songwriting, moving the Laurel Canyon sound toward smoother, LA-studio sophistication. It is the record most often cited as the bridge between confessional folk and the soft-rock mainstream of the mid-70s. Representative of how far the scene's polish could stretch without losing songwriting depth.
lineage: Continues Mitchell's folk-rock branch off V21/V22 songwriting traditions toward jazz-pop sophistication; leads into the smoothed-out LA session sound rather than back toward country rock's twang.

label: Asylum
description: A road-trip record built around Jaco Pastorius's fretless bass and Mitchell's open-tuned guitar, trading pop hooks for long, drifting, jazz-inflected meditations on travel and independence. It shows the Laurel Canyon songwriter moving furthest from the scene's radio-friendly center into art-song territory. A good deep-catalog landmark for listeners who already know Blue and Court and Spark.
lineage: Extends Mitchell's folk-rock branch (V21/V22-adjacent) into jazz fusion territory; a dead-end for country-rock purposes but influential on later art-folk songwriters outside the Core.

label: Atlantic Records
description: Three former band members' voices lock into the three-part harmony blueprint that defined Laurel Canyon folk rock, built on warm acoustic fingerpicking and easygoing tempos. It is the founding document of the soft-rock harmony sound before Neil Young joined for the electrified CSNY records already covered in the Core lineage. Essential for hearing the vocal-harmony half of the scene distinct from Young's guitar side.
lineage: Splits from the Byrds/Buffalo Springfield folk-rock lineage that also produced Cosmic American Music (V21) and the Crazy Horse/CSNY axis (V20/V22); this a cappella-harmony branch leads into the LA soft-rock mainstream rather than the twangier Core sound.

label: Asylum
description: Browne's stark, piano-and-guitar meditations on failing relationships and mortality set the introspective, plainly-sung template for LA singer-songwriter rock, with David Lindley's guitar work coloring every track. It is frequently cited as the peak of the confessional Laurel Canyon songwriter mode alongside Blue. A strong entry point for the lane's more melancholy, less country-inflected side.
lineage: Grows out of the same folk-revival and Cosmic American Music circles (V21) that shaped the Eagles and Linda Ronstadt; stays within the soft-rock singer-songwriter mainstream rather than crossing into twangier Core territory.

label: Asylum
description: A lusher, string-arranged follow-up written in the aftermath of personal tragedy, widening Browne's sound toward orchestral soft rock while keeping his plainspoken lyric voice. It shows the Laurel Canyon songwriter scene absorbing bigger studio budgets as the 70s wore on. A solid second Browne landmark for those who start with Late for the Sky.
lineage: Continues Browne's branch off the Laurel Canyon/Cosmic American Music songwriting scene (V21) into fuller studio-pop arrangements; remains in the soft-rock mainstream rather than the Core.

label: Asylum
description: A concept record recorded on the road, in hotel rooms and on the tour bus, turning the touring musician's life into song and blurring the line between live album and studio statement. It captures the Laurel Canyon scene's professional touring-band sound at its most road-worn and unguarded. An easy way in for listeners drawn to the 'life on the road' side of 70s soft rock.
lineage: Extends Browne's Laurel Canyon songwriting branch (V21-adjacent) into a road-diary live format that influenced later singer-songwriter tour records; stays outside the Core twang scene.

label: Asylum
description: The Eagles' debut, built by former Burrito Brothers and Poco sidemen, applies tight vocal harmonies and pedal steel to concise, radio-ready country-rock songs. It shows the same Cosmic American Music circle that produced the Byrds and Flying Burrito Brothers scaling the sound down into hit singles. A useful landmark for how country rock's rougher edges got smoothed into mainstream pop.
lineage: Splits directly from the Cosmic American Music/country rock lineage (V21) that this lane's parents share, trading V21's rawer twang for tighter pop songcraft; leads forward into the soft-rock mainstream rather than the Core.

label: Asylum
description: The Eagles' commercial and artistic peak trades their earlier country-rock twang for a darker, guitar-solo-driven arena-rock sound built around the title track's extended coda. It marks the point where LA soft rock became a global pop-culture phenomenon, for better and worse. Essential as the moment this branch left country rock behind entirely for stadium rock.
lineage: Completes the Eagles' drift away from V21's Cosmic American Music twang toward mainstream arena rock; the branch ends here rather than feeding back into the Core scene.

label: Capitol Records
description: Ronstadt's commercial breakthrough pairs her powerhouse voice with a crack Laurel Canyon studio band (Andrew Gold, JD Souther), covering country, pop and rock songs in a lush, pedal-steel-backed style. It became the model for the polished, interpretive side of country rock distinct from songwriter-driven records. A key landmark for how a covers-based singer could anchor the scene's sound.
lineage: Draws on the same Cosmic American Music session-player network (V21) that built the Eagles and Flying Burrito Brothers' sound; her interpretive, hit-single approach leads into mainstream pop-country rather than the twang Core.

label: Asylum Records
description: Ronstadt's biggest-selling record continues her interpretive country-rock approach with covers of Warren Zevon, Buddy Holly and the Rolling Stones alongside originals, backed by the same LA session-player crew heard on Eagles and Jackson Browne records. It epitomizes the late-70s soft-rock mainstream at its commercial peak. Good second landmark for the covers-and-craft half of the lane.
lineage: Continues Ronstadt's branch off the Cosmic American Music session scene (V21); stays in the mainstream pop-country lane rather than feeding the Core.

label: RCA
description: Nilsson's biggest commercial hit mixes barroom piano ballads, a hit cover ("Without You") and eccentric studio pop, sitting just outside the singer-songwriter mainstream of his Laurel Canyon peers thanks to his theatrical voice and studio-rat production choices. It shows the LA scene's more idiosyncratic, less country-adjacent wing. Useful contrast to the straighter country-rock records in this lane.
lineage: Runs parallel to the Laurel Canyon songwriter scene (V21/V22-adjacent) via shared LA studio circles and friendships with the Beatles and Randy Newman rather than a country-rock lineage; the branch leads into orchestral pop rather than toward the Core.

label: Sire
description: Fourteen buzzsaw songs in under half an hour, stripped to bare chords, deadpan vocals and cartoon-tough-guy lyrics, invented the American punk template almost single-handedly. Its speed, brevity and DIY simplicity became the foundation every SST and Dischord band after it worked from. The essential starting point for this whole lane.
lineage: Descends from the deadpan drone-and-amateurism ethos of the Velvet Underground and proto-indie scene (V29); this branch runs forward into hardcore, cowpunk and the SST/college-rock underground rather than continuing V29's own art-rock line.

label: Sire
description: A quick, tighter-sounding second album that keeps the debut's speed and joke-laden lyrics while sharpening the production slightly, proving the formula wasn't a one-off. It cemented the band's rapid album-a-year work rate that fed the DIY ethic later scenes copied. A solid second landmark for hearing the sound consolidate.
lineage: Continues the Ramones' branch off Velvet Underground deadpan minimalism (V29) toward the hardcore and DIY scenes that followed; not part of V29's own art-rock trajectory.

label: Sire
description: Often cited as the band's melodic peak, this third album layers surf and bubblegum-pop hooks onto the same buzzsaw formula, its highlights becoming genre standards covered for decades after. It shows the pop songcraft hiding inside the Ramones' minimalism that later power-pop and cowpunk bands drew on. A key third landmark rounding out the band's classic run.
lineage: Extends the Ramones' Velvet Underground-descended (V29) minimalist branch with stronger pop hooks, feeding forward into power pop and the DIY underground rather than back into V29's own catalog.

label: SST
description: Henry Rollins' first album with the band turns suburban California rage into lurching, brutal hardcore, self-released on Greg Ginn's own SST label after major distributors balked at it. It is the founding document of the SST/West Coast hardcore underground that the DIY network trunk line runs through. Essential for understanding where the SST label ethic that later shaped indie distribution began.
lineage: Splits from the New York punk template (this lane's Ramones/Dead Kennedys peers) into a harder, more nihilistic hardcore sound centered on Ginn's own label; feeds directly into the SST/college-rock underground (V16) rather than back toward V29.

label: SST
description: The infamous side two slows hardcore tempos to a doom-metal crawl, alienating the band's original audience but pointing directly at the slow, heavy sound that would become sludge and slowcore's noisier cousins. It shows SST hardcore mutating away from its own founding formula within a few years. A useful landmark for how quickly the scene's rules got broken from the inside.
lineage: Splits from Black Flag's own faster hardcore template (this lane) into slow, sludgy tempos that anticipate noise rock and slowcore textures; feeds forward into SST's own stranger later catalog and indirectly into post-punk/noise rock (X10) rather than back to the Core.

label: Dischord Records
description: Since Minor Threat never released a studio LP, this Dischord compilation collecting the band's two early-80s EPs (including the Minor Threat and Out of Step sessions) is the canonical way to hear Ian MacKaye's foundational straight-edge hardcore. Tight, fast and moralistic, it defined both the musical and ethical template (DIY labels, no drugs, no sellouts) that the whole American hardcore underground inherited. Essential for the DIY-network trunk line this lane sits under.
lineage: Descends from the same New York/DC hardcore acceleration of punk (alongside Bad Brains and Black Flag) that this lane covers; feeds directly into Dischord's DIY-label model and the American underground/college rock scene (V16) rather than back toward earlier UK or NY punk.

label: ROIR
description: A Washington, D.C. band of jazz-trained musicians plays hardcore at breakneck, technically dazzling speed and then drops into reggae interludes, originally released only on cassette by ROIR. Alongside Black Flag and Minor Threat it set the standard for early-80s American hardcore's intensity and musicianship. A key landmark showing the genre's virtuosic, genre-hopping edge.
lineage: Runs alongside Minor Threat and Black Flag in the DC/West Coast hardcore acceleration of punk; feeds into the American hardcore underground (V16) and later crossover thrash rather than back toward V29's art-rock roots.

label: CBS/Epic
description: The Clash's genre-sprawling double album folds rockabilly, reggae, ska and R&B into a punk base, proving the genre could absorb roots music without losing its edge. That genre-mixing openness, including its own flirtations with Americana-tinged rockabilly, fed directly into the cowpunk bands that followed on the US side. Included here as the UK punk landmark that most directly informed cowpunk's genre-crossing instincts.
lineage: Represents the UK punk scene running alongside this lane's American hardcore lineage; its genre-blending approach (rockabilly, reggae) feeds forward into cowpunk and LA roots punk (V14) alongside the Ramones' more direct hardcore influence.

label: Cherry Red Records
description: Jello Biafra's surf-guitar-inflected San Francisco hardcore debut pairs breakneck tempos with pointed political satire aimed at Reagan-era California, released independently through the band's own Alternative Tentacles operation. It stands alongside Black Flag as a founding text of West Coast hardcore's DIY, self-released model. Essential for the political-satire wing of the punk foundation this lane covers.
lineage: Runs parallel to Black Flag's Southern California hardcore scene under the same DIY, self-released model; feeds the American hardcore underground (V16) and the broader DIY network trunk line rather than back toward V29.

label: Frontier Records
description: Fourteen songs blaze past in fifteen minutes on this LA hardcore debut, formed by an ex-Black Flag singer and stripped down to pure speed and sneering humor. Its extreme brevity and DIY release on the independent Frontier label made it one of the era's most-cited hardcore landmarks. A tight, essential companion to Damaged for the early-80s LA hardcore scene.
lineage: Grows directly out of the same Hermosa Beach/LA hardcore scene as Black Flag (a former member founded the band); feeds the American hardcore underground (V16) and DIY network rather than back into earlier NY punk.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Will Johnson (Centro-matic, South San Gabriel, Monsters of Folk) sings in a craggy, weathered rasp over spare, atmospheric folk-rock built from acoustic guitar, brushed drums and low organ drones. It is unhurried, private-feeling songwriting, closer to a late-night confession than a rock record.
lineage: Johnson's solo work extends the Secretly Canadian/Jason Molina-adjacent lineage of haunted, Crazy Horse-scaled Americana into a quieter solo register.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A hushed, largely solo-recorded set named for the Spanish Civil War and other historical fragments, matching Johnson's plainspoken baritone to spare guitar and occasional strings. It sits at the quiet, wounded end of his catalog.
lineage: Continues the same Molina/Centro-matic-adjacent lineage as Johnson's other solo records.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Desert-toned cosmic country from an Austin band steeped in Marfa mysticism: reverb-heavy pedal steel, loping tempos and Shannon's high, reedy voice drifting over slow-building arrangements.
lineage: Part of the 2010s Austin cosmic-country revival alongside Twain and Promised Land Sound, drawing on Gram Parsons-style country rock filtered through desert psychedelia.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Three-song EP of slow-motion, synth-tinged dream-folk from Carly Bond's San Francisco project: sparse arrangements, cavernous reverb and a fragile, close-mic'd vocal at the center.
lineage: Extends Meernaa's hushed, slowcore-adjacent songwriting between Duster-style haze and modern indie folk.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Mat Davidson's twain project sets a high, keening voice against loose, fingerpicked country-folk with occasional bursts of full-band warmth. It's intimate cosmic country, closer to a campfire than a road trip.
lineage: Davidson's songwriting draws directly on Gram Parsons-style cosmic country and old-time singing, filtered through a DIY, small-label folk scene.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A warmer, more full-band twain record than its predecessors, still built around Davidson's reedy tenor but adding lightly psychedelic guitar textures and looser tempos.
lineage: Continues the cosmic-country lineage of Rare Feeling with a slightly fuller studio palette.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Why Bonnie's debut full-length trades their earlier bedroom dream-pop for raw-edged, feedback-streaked indie rock; frontwoman Blair Howerton has cited Townes Van Zandt and Blaze Foley alongside the Replacements and Sparklehorse as touchstones for its road-trip-through-Texas songwriting.
lineage: A Texas band's move from dream pop toward a more country-and-alt-rock-inflected sound, echoing the wider indie-twang turn without being a straight country record.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Hushed, minor-key indie folk built from finger-picked guitar and Lucille's airy, wavering voice, with lyrics circling grief and the underworld (the title nods to Persephone's myth).
lineage: Sits in the 2010s Austin/Bandcamp indie-folk scene alongside labelmates Rae Fitzgerald and Erin Durant.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A dreamy, lo-fi debut from a Louisiana songwriter working partly in French, mixing Cajun-inflected folk melody with woozy, four-track-style production.
lineage: Draws on South Louisiana's French-language folk tradition filtered through a hushed, Bandcamp-era indie-folk sensibility.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Piano-led songs from a former touring keyboardist (Jenny Lewis, Phosphorescent) stepping into her own material: slow-building, emotionally direct arrangements built around Schornikow's plainspoken alto.
lineage: A session-musician's turn to solo songwriting, closer in spirit to the piano-based end of indie folk/slowcore than to any single scene.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Jazzy, warm-toned folk from a New Orleans songwriter, mixing loose acoustic guitar and piano with unhurried melodic turns that owe as much to Randy Newman as to any folk revivalist.
lineage: Grows out of Durant's New Orleans singer-songwriter background before her later, more country-facing Ruination Record Co. records.

label: Tell 'Em Tapes
description: A six-song, lo-fi indie-folk EP of intimate, close-mic'd acoustic songs from an Austin songwriter later signed to Keeled Scales.
lineage: Part of the same Austin DIY-folk circle as Julia Lucille and RF Shannon.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A 28-track compilation of Aaron Dowdy's earliest home-recorded songs (2017-2018), released as a single sprawling document years before Fust became a full band. Rough four-track country songs, drum-machine and all, that show the roots of the band's later, more polished storytelling.
lineage: Predates and directly seeds the full-band Fust sound heard on Genevieve and Big Ugly; a look at the songwriter's home-recording origins before the Dear Life Records band era.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A shifting North Carolina old-time/DIY-noise collective (members of Sluice and Magic Tuber Stringband among them) recording traditional ballads and hymns with tape manipulation and found-sound production, cut live at a family dairy farm in Virginia.
lineage: Bridges the Piedmont old-time/string-band tradition with the same DIY network that produces Sluice and Fust, treating inherited folk songs as raw material for experimental production.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Michael Cormier-O'Leary's chamber-folk ensemble Hour expands to a 13-piece orchestra of winds, strings and vibraphone for a slow, meditative suite about disappearance and loss, closer to instrumental chamber music than a rock record.
lineage: Cormier-O'Leary also founded Dear Life Records and plays in Friendship and 2nd Grade, tying Hour directly into the same Philadelphia deadpan/slowcore circle.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A 15-track live album stitched together from two years of DIY touring, capturing Hour's shifting chamber-folk ensemble across bars, movie theaters and living rooms.
lineage: A touring-diary capstone to Hour's catalog before Ghost Bridge, part of the same Dear Life Records/Cormier-O'Leary world as Friendship and 2nd Grade.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Dave Benton's Trace Mountains project leans further into pedal-steel-flecked, warmly recorded country-pop on this record, mixing jangling guitars with synths and unhurried melodies.
lineage: A former LVL UP member's move toward twangier, more countryish songwriting, part of the same Brooklyn/Lame-O indie scene as Slaughter Beach, Dog.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Matt Scottoline's Hurry project debut: tight, hook-forward power pop with an easy, unfussy jangle, plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and self-doubt.
lineage: Part of the same Philadelphia power-pop revival as 2nd Grade and Golden Apples, descended from Big Star and Superchunk.

label: Lame-O Records
description: A sprawling 20-song double set of concise, hook-driven power pop split into 'Girls' and 'Boys' halves, led by Peter Gill (also of Friendship and Hour).
lineage: Continues 2nd Grade's Big Star/Guided by Voices-indebted songwriting within the same Dear Life/Lame-O Philadelphia scene as Friendship and Hurry.

label: Lame-O Records
description: A brief, three-song burst of ringing, mid-fi guitar pop from another corner of Lame-O's Philadelphia power-pop stable, all hooks and no filler in under seven minutes total.
lineage: Part of the same Philadelphia jangle-pop scene as Hurry and 2nd Grade.

label: Alive Naturalsound Records
description: A laid-back homage to '70s Topanga Canyon and Marin County sounds from a band built around former Beachwood Sparks players: jangly, country-tinged FM rock full of easy harmonies.
lineage: Formed by Beachwood Sparks/Jonny Niemann/Neal Casal alumni, directly continuing the Paisley Underground-to-cosmic-country lineage that Curation Records now catalogs.

label: Curation
description: The Paisley Underground/cosmic-country pioneers' first album in over a decade, mixing pedal-steel-laced country rock with the band's longtime cosmic, harmony-driven sound.
lineage: A late-career return from one of the foundational 2000s cosmic-country/Paisley Underground revival bands (V15/C6's direct lineage), now released on their own reissue-and-new-music label.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: A young Nashville band's second album, expanding from garage-country burners into ambitious, Byrds/Big Star-indebted psych-country with guest guitar from Steve Gunn.
lineage: Nashville's 2010s cosmic-country underground, tied to Paradise of Bachelors' wider American-vernacular roster and to Steve Gunn's Black Dirt Studio circle.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: Erin Birgy's surrealist song-world turns painterly and desert-lit on this record, co-produced with Big Thief's James Krivchenia: avant-pop arrangements wrapped around plainspoken, image-dense lyrics.
lineage: Connected to the Big Thief/indie-folk network via Krivchenia's production; sits at the arty edge of the twangy indie-folk lane.

label: Orindal Records
description: A Chicago multi-instrumentalist's (Ohmme, Marker) solo debut: spare piano- and violin-inflected songs recorded mostly alone, moving between chamber-folk intimacy and quiet dissonance.
lineage: Grows out of Chicago's overlapping indie-folk/experimental scene, tied to Orindal labelmates Gia Margaret and Macie Stewart's other Chicago projects.

label: Keeled Scales / Orindal Records
description: A Tucson artist's solo-produced record blending Americana-tinged songwriting with ambient sound design: synthesizer, tape loops, field recordings and her own desert-referencing lyrics.
lineage: A joint release between Keeled Scales and Orindal Records, connecting Tucson's desert-folk scene to both labels' networks.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Durant's most recent record continues her warm, jazz-inflected folk songwriting, now on the Brooklyn label Ruination Record Co.
lineage: A later-career continuation of the same New Orleans folk songwriting heard on her earlier Keeled Scales record Islands.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Dan Knishkowy's Adeline Hotel project offers gentle, fingerpicked indie folk with plainspoken, slightly wry lyrics about memory and routine.
lineage: Part of a small Brooklyn/Ruination songwriter circle (Frank Meadows, Jackie West, The Bird Calls) that frequently collaborates across each other's records.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: A Brooklyn songwriter's guitar-and-synth indie rock record, made with a rotating cast from the same Ruination/Adeline Hotel circle (Dan Knishkowy, Katie Von Scheicher).
lineage: Part of the same small Brooklyn songwriter-collaborator scene as Adeline Hotel, Office Culture and The Bird Calls.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Sam Sodomsky's songwriting project draws explicit comparison to David Berman, John Darnielle and Destroyer's Dan Bejar: clever, plainspoken songs balancing folksy earnestness against wry self-awareness.
lineage: A direct continuation of the Drag City deadpan-songwriter lineage (Berman, Darnielle) within the small Brooklyn Ruination/Adeline Hotel circle.
key_tracks: To Everything There Is A Ceiling

album: Say a Prayer to the Gods of Getting Going
label: Polyvinyl
description: A travel-inspired record balancing Williams's enveloping voice against crunchy, wall-of-guitar live production, drawing comparisons to Wednesday and Alex G.
lineage: Continues Squirrel Flower's move toward the countrygaze-adjacent, guitar-wall sound of Wednesday's circle.

label: Sugar Free Records
description: Beulah's second album pairs Elephant 6-style horn charts and layered harmonies with a scrappier, more rock-leaning backbone than their debut. Miles Kurosky's bittersweet melodies and off-kilter brass arrangements sit over loose, unpolished guitar pop. It's for listeners who want the Elephant 6 sound without the whimsy tipping into twee.
lineage: Grew out of the Elephant 6 collective alongside Apples in Stereo and Olivia Tremor Control; its warm, horn-laced melancholy fed later indie-pop and slacker-pop bands drawing on '60s pop craft.

label: spinART
description: The Minders' debut is chiming, lo-fi guitar pop cut from the same Elephant 6 cloth as Neutral Milk Hotel and Apples in Stereo, with Martyn Leaper's reedy vocals riding fuzzed, melodic hooks. Production is homemade and a little wobbly, favoring hummable tunes over polish. A good entry point for the collective's sunnier, less psychedelic wing.
lineage: Formed within the Elephant 6 collective (Leaper played with the Apples in Stereo); its scrappy jangle-pop feeds the same lo-fi indie-pop lineage as Guided by Voices and the Olivia Tremor Control.

label: Work Records
description: A former Boston subway busker's only major-label album, pairing her plainspoken, slightly nasal voice with jangly folk-rock arrangements and songs co-written with Nick Saloman (the Bevis Frond) and Freedy Johnston. It leans more toward '90s college-radio jangle-pop than lo-fi slacker rock, closer in spirit to Liz Phair's guest spot on the record.
lineage: Emerged from the Boston indie/busking scene around Bevis Frond and Elliott Smith (who contributed to her earlier EPs); represents the more polished, radio-adjacent edge of '90s indie jangle.
key_tracks: Some Jingle Jangle Morning (When I'm Straight)

label: Harvest
description: Chapman's debut LP is psychedelic-tinged British folk-guitar songwriting, produced by Gus Dudgeon, with his weathered baritone over fingerpicked and occasionally full-band arrangements. It opens with his best-known song, "It Didn't Work Out," and moves through wistful, understated ballads. A key entry point into the British folk-rock guitar tradition that indie folk and American Primitive players still cite.
lineage: Part of the same late-60s UK folk-guitar wave as Bert Jansch and Nick Drake; Chapman's fingerstyle playing directly influenced American Primitive guitarists and later indie-folk songwriters.

label: Flying Nun / Homestead
description: Graeme Downes and the Verlaines' second album pairs the Dunedin sound's homemade, chiming guitars with unusually literate, classically-informed songwriting and a raw, garage-recorded punch. Tracks jump between full-band jangle and stripped-back drama, with Downes's cracked, urgent voice carrying it. Essential listening for the Flying Nun catalog's more ambitious songwriting wing.
lineage: Core Dunedin sound / Flying Nun band alongside the Chills and the Clean; its homemade jangle and drone fed the American college-rock and lo-fi scenes that picked up Flying Nun records via Homestead's US distribution.

label: See Thru Broadcasting (US) / Chemikal Underground (UK)
description: Radar Bros.' second album is slow, reverb-soaked guitar rock built on Jim Putnam's murmured vocals and unhurried tempos, closer to Codeine or Duster than to Pavement's scrappier slacker sound. Long, patient song structures and warm analog production give it a hazy, half-asleep quality. A good pick for listeners drawn to '90s indie's quieter, sadder corner.
lineage: Grew out of the LA indie scene alongside Grandaddy (whom Putnam later joined); its slow-motion guitar rock sits at the crossroads of Matador/Merge-style slacker indie and the slowcore/sadcore lineage of Codeine and Bedhead.

label: Homestead
description: Salem 66's third album pairs the twin vocals of Judy Grunwald and Beth Kaplan over ringing, mid-tempo guitar rock, part of Homestead Records' Boston-area roster. It leans folkier and more melodic than the label's noisier acts, with plainspoken lyrics and close, conversational harmonies. A representative slice of American underground/college-rock's gentler wing.
lineage: Boston Homestead-label peers of Dinosaur Jr. and Salem 66's own earlier work with Sonic Youth's Lee Ranaldo producing; part of the SST/Homestead college-radio network that fed the later lo-fi and Bandcamp DIY scene.

album: Naked at the Buy, Sell and Trade
label: Homestead
description: Columbus, Ohio's Great Plains play scrappy, deadpan guitar-pop stuffed with pop-culture jokes and rapid-fire wordplay, closer to a Midwestern update of the Feelies than to hardcore. Ron House's flat, wry vocal delivery over jangly, fast-strummed guitars anticipates the funny-sad Drag City school. A key document of the '80s Homestead/college-rock underground outside the coasts.
lineage: Part of the same Homestead/college-radio underground as the Feelies and R.E.M.; House's deadpan, joke-laced songwriting is a direct forerunner of the Drag City deadpan school (Silver Jews, Pavement).

label: Big Time
description: Boston's Christmas play jittery, hook-heavy college rock with Michael Cudahy's deadpan, absurdist lyrics riding bright, angular guitars. It's brasher and more new-wave-inflected than its underground peers, with a cartoonish energy that never loses the tunes. A good example of '80s college rock's stranger, funnier fringe.
lineage: Part of the Boston college-rock scene alongside the Pixies' early circuit; its jokey, deadpan lyricism sits in the same lineage that runs toward the Drag City school's funny-sad songwriting.

label: DB Records
description: Love Tractor's debut is mostly instrumental, twangy post-punk jangle from the same early-80s Athens, Georgia scene that produced R.E.M. and Pylon. Interlocking guitar lines and a loose, homemade feel give it a warm, unhurried character rare among their punkier peers. A key document of Athens' guitar-forward, DIY college-rock beginnings.
lineage: Formed within the Athens, GA scene alongside R.E.M. and Pylon, sharing members and stages; its ringing, interlocking guitars are a direct antecedent of the jangle strand of American underground/college rock.

label: Rough Trade
description: Scrawl's second album is rough, unglamorous Midwestern guitar rock led by Marcy Mays' and Sue Harshe's plainspoken, alternately deadpan and shouted vocals. The playing is loose and live-sounding, closer to a bar band than a studio project, with blunt lyrics about drinking and bad relationships. A rawer, more female-fronted counterpart to labelmates like the Replacements.
lineage: Columbus, Ohio underground contemporaries of Great Plains; part of the same Homestead/Rough Trade-era college-rock network that fed the '90s slacker and lo-fi scenes.

label: DB Records
description: Bobby Sutliff and Tim Lee's Mississippi band play bright, Byrds-descended jangle-pop with tight vocal harmonies and clean, ringing guitar interplay. It's more melodic and pop-focused than their noisier Southern college-rock peers, closer to Let's Active than to Pylon. A key example of the South's own strand of '80s American jangle/college rock.
lineage: Part of the same DB Records / Southern college-rock network as R.E.M. and Let's Active; its clean jangle-pop is a direct ancestor of '90s power-pop and jangle bands.

label: Flying Nun
description: The Clean guitarist's second solo album is warmer and more song-based than his band's drone-heavy jangle, with hushed vocals over unhurried, softly fuzzed guitar melodies. The homemade production keeps the Dunedin sound's lo-fi character while leaning toward gentle pop songcraft. A good solo counterpart to the Clean's more driving records.
lineage: Extends the Dunedin sound / Flying Nun lineage he helped define with the Clean; its quiet, homemade jangle feeds directly into '90s and 2000s lo-fi indie pop internationally.

label: Folkways Records
description: Mike Seeger, John Cohen and Tom Paley's debut recreates 1920s-30s old-time string-band music note-for-note off 78s, revivalists playing traditional fiddle, banjo and mandolin tunes and songs with scholarly fidelity. It's plainly recorded and unadorned, meant to preserve the source material rather than reinterpret it. A foundational document of the postwar old-time revival that runs directly into the folk revival's roots consciousness.
lineage: Drew directly on Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music and prewar string-band 78s; the group's scholarly revivalism fed the 1960s folk revival and every later old-time/roots-conscious songwriter who dug into pre-war sources.
key_tracks: Don't Let Your Deal Go Down

label: MCA
description: Ely's early-80s MCA album pushes his Lubbock roots-rock toward new-wave-inflected production, with synths and drum machines alongside his Telecaster twang and rasping voice. It's a stranger, more experimental record than his earlier Texas honky-tonk albums, chasing a rootsy new-wave crossover in the vein of Joe King Carrasco. A curiosity for fans tracing how '80s country outsiders wrestled with mainstream rock production.
lineage: Part of the Flatlanders/Lubbock songwriter circle with Butch Hancock and Jimmie Dale Gilmore; Ely's restless border-rock songwriting fed the alt-country and Americana movements of the '90s.
key_tracks: Locked In A Boxcar With The Queen Of Spain

label: Palace Records
description: A Louisville side project of Will Oldham associates (Jack Carneal, Paul Oldham), this debut sets classic Mother Goose nursery rhymes to hushed, homemade country-folk arrangements. Short, plainly sung and gently strummed, it reads as a lo-fi lullaby record rather than a conventional singer-songwriter statement. An oddball but genuine offshoot of the Palace/Drag City circle's deadpan, homespun aesthetic.
lineage: Direct offshoot of Will Oldham's Palace Records world, sharing members and a label with Palace Music; part of the Drag City deadpan school's more experimental, lo-fi fringe.

label: Gnomonsong
description: Recorded with the indie-folk band Ida, this Gnomonsong release (the label run by Vetiver's Andy Cabic and Devendra Banhart) frames Hurley's rambling country-blues songs in gentle full-band arrangements. His cracked, easygoing voice stays the center, but the backing is warmer and fuller than his solo records. A good look at how the 2000s freak-folk generation embraced him as an elder statesman.
lineage: Part of the 2000s freak-folk/New Weird America rediscovery of Hurley by artists like Vetiver and Devendra Banhart; extends his direct influence on the Drag City deadpan-folk lineage into a new generation.
key_tracks: I Stole The Right To Live

label: Flying Nun Records
description: Formed by two ex-members of the Gordons, Bailter Space's debut trades the Dunedin sound's chime for churning, noise-caked guitar rock, closer to Flying Nun's harder, feedback-driven edge. Vocals are buried and monotone under waves of distortion and heavy, motorik rhythms. A key bridge between New Zealand's DIY guitar scene and the noisier post-punk/shoegaze lineage.
lineage: Grew out of Christchurch post-punk pioneers the Gordons; its noise-wall guitar sound anticipates both Flying Nun's noisier 90s bands and the international shoegaze/noise-rock scene.

label: Self-released
description: This Sydney band's debut is scrappy, conversational lo-fi indie pop, recorded cheaply with shifting vocalists trading deadpan, half-spoken lines over loose, ramshackle arrangements. It shares the homemade DIY spirit of Flying Nun's Dunedin bands but with a drier, more Australian sense of humor. An early document of the Antipodean lo-fi/DIY network that fed international college radio.
lineage: Part of the same Antipodean DIY-indie network as the Flying Nun bands, later closely tied to Chicago's lo-fi scene via shared members and releases; its homemade aesthetic connects directly to the SST/college-radio-to-Bandcamp DIY lineage.

label: Self-released
description: After leaving the Jayhawks, Mark Olson and his wife Victoria Williams recorded this desert-folk debut at home in Joshua Tree with a loose collective of friends. It's hushed, harmony-rich country-folk built on acoustic guitars and warm, communal singing, far more homespun than Olson's Jayhawks work. A foundational record for the loose Joshua Tree desert-folk scene that fed the 2000s cosmic-country/Americana revival.
lineage: Grew directly out of Mark Olson's departure from the Jayhawks and Victoria Williams's Americana songwriting; the Creekdippers' communal, desert-recorded sound anticipated the 2010s cosmic-country/Cosmic American Music revival.

label: Liberty & Lament
description: On this 2023 album Lucero keep the boozy, horn-flecked Memphis rock-and-soul sound of their 2010s records, with Ben Nichols's gravelly voice carrying weary, plainspoken songs about aging and regret. Tempos stay mid-paced and the arrangements lean on organ and horns as much as guitar. A late-career entry that finds the band settled into their barroom-soul identity.
lineage: Long-running Memphis band whose punk-to-Southern-rock arc runs parallel to the Drive-By Truckers; part of the same storytelling Southern-rock lineage that feeds bands like Wednesday and Tyler Childers.

label: Tender Loving Empire
description: CARE/TAKING is Jess Cornelius's plainspoken solo record, ten songs about caregiving, distance and loss set over spare, folk-leaning arrangements. Formerly of Teeth & Tongue, the Australian-American songwriter favors quiet observation over drama.
lineage: A solo continuation of Cornelius's move from Melbourne indie rock toward hushed, Los Angeles-recorded singer-songwriter folk.

label: Arts & Crafts
description: Stay in Touch is Georgia Harmer's stunning debut, an eleven-song set that spans intimate folk and strummy country to jazz-inflected pop-rock, recorded live-feeling in a West Toronto garage. Her lyrics capture fleeting, specific moments with unusual poise for a songwriter barely out of her teens.
lineage: Daughter of Canadian roots singer Sarah Harmer, extending that lineage into a 2020s indie-folk idiom on the Arts & Crafts roster.

label: Fire Talk Records
description: Leaving is Maria Jacobson's second album as Fran, eleven songs of loss and possibility written through pandemic isolation and questions of faith. Clarinet drones and delicate strings wrap around Jacobson's plainspoken, questioning voice.
lineage: Part of the Fire Talk roster alongside Slow Pulp and Horse Jumper of Love, extending Chicago's hushed, folk-leaning strand of indie rock.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Close To The Mystery was recorded live at Brooklyn's Figure 8 Studios with a cast that includes Shahzad Ismaily and Sarah Pedinotti, twelve unhurried songs of patient, detail-rich folk rock. Jackie West's guitar and voice sit at the center of loose, warm full-band arrangements.
lineage: Shares its label, Ruination Record Co., with Blue Ranger, part of a small roster of patient, collaborative New York folk-rock records.

album: in filth your mystery is kingdom / far smile peasant in yellow music
label: AD 93
description: Originally self-uploaded to Bandcamp in obscurity before reaching Phil Elverum and getting a proper reissue on AD 93, this debut is ghostly, home-recorded folk built from spectral harmonies and muted synths. It is intimate to the point of eavesdropping, closer to a private tape than a studio record.
lineage: A DIY-to-reissue story in the mold of Elverum's own Microphones/Mount Eerie catalog, tying Mexico City's lo-fi folk underground to the wider hushed-recording network this lane tracks.
key_tracks: In Filth Your Mystery Is Kingdom
Even God Gets Stuck In Devotion

label: Western Vinyl
description: Lamplight is Ian Hatcher-Williams' debut under the name, pastoral folk rock made intricate and immediate by Kevin Copeland's (Lightning Bug) deft, dreamlike production. Its nine songs move between hope and panic, confrontation and avoidance, closing on a tender message of self-acceptance.
lineage: Produced by Lightning Bug's Kevin Copeland, tying Lamplight to that band's hazy, Western Vinyl-adjacent strand of indie folk.

label: Thirty Tigers / Miss Freedomland
description: Halfsies is Lizzie No's charming, infectious concept album of modern Americana, eleven songs that close by way of a rich, genre-fluid songwriting voice honed on the Cosmic Country Showcase circuit. It balances pedal-steel warmth with sharp, personal storytelling.
lineage: No's own Miss Freedomland imprint and the Cosmic Country Showcase she co-hosts tie her to the wider Black country and cosmic-country revival within this lane's neighboring C3 scene.

label: Self-released
description: This Is Music is a stripped-back, conversational solo record recorded in three days, klark sound's pristine croon sitting somewhere between Labi Siffre and Fleet Foxes' Robin Pecknold over spare acoustic arrangements.
lineage: A quiet, self-recorded entry in the same hushed singer-songwriter vein as Otto Benson and Jessica Risker.

label: Tiny Library Records
description: Lily of the Valley is Will Kennedy's second 22º Halo album, nine vivacious, hopeful songs written through a partner's brain-cancer diagnosis. It sits between folk, slacker rock and bedroom pop, its plainspoken hush carrying real weight without turning maudlin.
lineage: Part of Philadelphia's DIY scene overlapping Friendship and hemlock's Orindal/Double Yolk circle, extending that city's hushed, homemade strand of indie folk.

album: I See Them, I See Me
label: Double Double Whammy
description: I See Them, I See Me finds Maya Bon's Babehoven pushing into full-band indie folk-pop with country and Americana touches, its soaring vocals and explosive production a marked step up from the duo's lo-fi beginnings. It keeps the emotional directness of earlier records while widening the arrangements.
lineage: Babehoven's studio (run with Ryan Albert) has become a hub for this lane's hushed-folk network, having co-produced Bloomsday's Heart of the Artichoke; this album marks their own move toward a fuller, more countrified sound.

label: Bayonet Records
description: Heart of the Artichoke is Iris James Garrison's delicate, perceptive record about connection and healing, spacious full-bodied folk songs recorded in ten days upstate at Babehoven's studio. Earworm melodies and a wide cast of collaborators (Lomelda's Andrew Stevens, h.pruz, Babehoven's Maya Bon) give it warmth without excess polish.
lineage: Co-produced by Babehoven's Ryan Albert and mixed by Slow Pulp's Henry Stoehr, tying Bloomsday directly into this lane's hushed-folk collaborator network.

label: Self-released
description: Body is a dynamic debut swinging from homespun quiet to raging catharsis, Elliott Smith, Pinback and Owen touchpoints filtered through natural, unpolished harmonies. Its eleven songs favor emotional whiplash over consistency of mood.
lineage: Sits at the emo-adjacent, slowcore-leaning edge of this lane, closer to Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer than to overt twang.

label: Self-released
description: Sounds is Mark Scott's side project apart from villagerrr, eleven hushed, lo-fi songs with titles like 'Daniel Boone' and 'Buc-ees' that lean into a wandering, small-town Americana feel. It is looser and more homemade than villagerrr's main output.
lineage: A side outlet for villagerrr's Mark Scott, released on his own Bandcamp alongside that band's catalog.

label: Self-released
description: Imbecile is an early, self-recorded document from Boone Patrello's Dead Sullivan project, eleven raw, hushed songs made before Patrello went on to co-found the Texas slowcore band Teethe. It is rougher and more diaristic than his later work.
lineage: A direct predecessor to Teethe, tying Dead Sullivan to the same Texas slowcore lineage that runs through this lane.

label: Fire Talk Records
description: into a pretty room is Newcastle duo Billy Woodhouse and Elliot Dryden's Fire Talk debut, a winsome, ramshackle collage of reworked bedroom demos, flickering electronics and processed vocals about grief, growing up and letting go.
lineage: Shares Fire Talk Records with Bnny and Fran, extending that label's hushed, home-recorded strand of indie rock to the UK.

label: Self-released
description: Any Light is a sophisticated, deliberately paced folk record from Victoria, BC's Loving, ten unhurried songs built on close harmony and patient arrangement. It favors restraint over hooks, rewarding slow, careful listening.
lineage: A Canadian counterpart to the hushed American folk-rock this lane tracks, working at its own unhurried pace outside any particular scene.

label: Drag City
description: Mess Esque's third album is a twisted, handmade folk record from Helen Franzmann (McKisko) and Mick Turner (Dirty Three), eight songs that build a warm, dreamlike world out of plainspoken vocals and loose, unhurried arrangements. It sounds openhearted and slightly askew at once.
lineage: Released on Drag City, placing Mess Esque squarely within that label's deadpan, wry songwriting lineage alongside Bill Callahan and Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.

label: Self-released
description: The Spot is a stripped-back, wistfully optimistic bedroom-pop record cut in upstate New York, nine brief songs favoring hushed, homemade warmth over polish.
lineage: A small, self-recorded entry in the same breezy, low-key bedroom-folk vein as klark sound and kitship.

label: 7 e.p.
description: Four Days in June has Joseph Shabason and Nicholas Krgovich reaching for CD-era songcraft in the vein of Neil Young's Harvest Moon and k.d. lang, its brushed drums and understated pedal steel, banjo and fiddle (courtesy of guest Sam Amidon) giving their usual wry chamber-pop a country-rock glow.
lineage: Named after Blue Rodeo's alt-country landmark Five Days in July, this record openly borrows from 90s pop-country and Cosmic American touchstones while keeping the duo's own understated, plainspoken songwriting.

label: Self-released
description: Marketplace is the debut from Fort Wayne trio The Namby Pamby, eight tracks of sparse but pretty slow-burn indie rock recorded locally at Off the Cuff Sound. It favors patient builds and understated melody over hooks.
lineage: A small-market Midwest counterpart to the slowcore-adjacent bands (Horse Jumper of Love, Teethe) this lane tracks.

album: Well Once There Was A King
label: Historic NJ Recordings
description: A sprawling, 24-song grab-bag from an Oregon home-recording project, Well Once There Was A King cycles through folk, slacker jangle, country, doom-metal detours and Beach Boys harmonies without pausing for breath. It rewards the same magpie curiosity that draws people to Guided by Voices' overstuffed records.
lineage: Descends from the lo-fi, kitchen-sink home-taping tradition of GBV and Sebadoh, filtered through a 2020s Bandcamp DIY sensibility.

label: Fat Possum
description: A stark breakup record built from voice, piano and pedal steel, Old Flowers is Courtney Marie Andrews at her most unadorned, with a Ronstadt-range voice carrying every ounce of the heartbreak. It's the record that crossed her from journeyman Americana singer to a defining voice of the 2010s-20s twangy-folk revival.
lineage: Bridges 1970s Laurel Canyon songwriting (Ronstadt, Mitchell) into the modern indie-folk scene; her later records lean further into full-band cosmic country.

label: Fat Possum
description: Loose Future opens Courtney Marie Andrews back up into full-band, '70s-Nashville-flavored arrangements after the bare-bones Old Flowers, with buttery lead guitar and warm harmonies replacing the earlier record's silence.
lineage: A direct continuation of the country-rock/Cosmic American Music lineage, following her own path from stripped-down folk into the cosmic country revival.
key_tracks: These Are the Good Old Days

label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
description: Dean Johnson sings timeless, uncluttered cowboy waltzes in a soulful tenor that recalls classic countrypolitan records more than any indie trend. Nothing for Me, Please is spare and patient, letting his voice and the pedal steel do the emotional work.
lineage: Sits in the singer-songwriter lineage of 1970s country balladeers, adopted by the 2020s indie-folk scene via Mama Bird's Pacific Northwest roster.

label: St. Itch
description: Ellie O'Neill's debut sets calm, alto-led vocals against austere, minimalist arrangements that occasionally bloom into ornate pastoral rock. Touchstones like Laura Marling and Joni Mitchell are audible, but Time of Fallow's Irish folk grounding and biblical imagery give it its own hushed gravity.
lineage: Draws on British/Irish folk-rock songwriting (Fairport Convention, Sandy Denny) reframed through the 2020s international indie-folk scene.

label: Patchwork Label
description: Gawshock makes quiet, homespun Southern indie folk out of Huntsville, Alabama, the kind of unhurried songwriting that favors atmosphere and repetition over hooks. Leaves to the Sun continues the lo-fi thread of the project's earlier self-titled record and Unless If EP.
lineage: A small-town Southern branch of the Bandcamp DIY folk network, feeding the same audience as other regional home-recording projects covered by No Expectations.

label: Mtn Laurel Recording Co.
description: Hannah Pruzinsky's second album, co-produced by Florist/Told Slant's Felix Walworth, threads Wurlitzer, saxophone and synth through an explorative, quiet folk framework. Red sky at morning is a meditation on love, control and domesticity that never raises above a gentle murmur.
lineage: Grows directly out of the Florist/Told Slant hushed-folk orbit that also feeds Modern Slowcore's C8 lane.

label: Luminelle Recordings
description: Helena Deland's second album pairs graceful, evocative songwriting with delicate acoustic arrangements and glittering Sam Evian production. It's smart, literary indie folk more than straight twang, but its acoustic-led intimacy places it alongside the wider 2020s Bandcamp folk revival.
lineage: A Montreal singer-songwriter lineage that runs parallel to Ada Lea and other Canadian indie-folk artists of the same scene.

label: Self-released
description: kitship's am i a rock? is eight low-key songs of acoustic singer-songwriter fare and understated lo-fi indie rock, built on commanding vocals and instant, unfussy melodies. A guest spot from Sharp Pins ties it into Chicago's current DIY guitar-pop scene.
lineage: Part of the current Chicago Bandcamp slacker/lo-fi network that also includes Sharp Pins.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: Raised in Appalachian Pennsylvania and nicknamed "The Rose of Appalachia" for her clawhammer banjo playing, Angela Autumn folds American folk and bluegrass roots into a hybridized, arena-sized sound on Believer, blending indie, psychedelia and gothic country.
lineage: Grows out of Appalachian old-time and bluegrass tradition, recast through the 2020s cosmic-country revival's bigger, more psychedelic production.

label: YK Records
description: Annie Williams's debut is a refreshing, tasteful set of subtle pop melodies and conversational, funny writing, arranged sparsely by a crew of Nashville session players. Visitor favors wit and understatement over big hooks.
lineage: Part of the current Nashville indie-folk underground built around small labels like YK Records.

label: Mtn Laurel Recording Co.
description: A member of the band TOLEDO, Aïda Mekonnen Caby steps out with pristine, dreamy folk-pop dressed in the same big-indie production polish as her main band, but at a more intimate, personal scale on Mais Uma.
lineage: Feeds off the TOLEDO/Winspear-adjacent Brooklyn indie-pop scene while drawing on folk songwriting fundamentals.

label: Tiny Engines
description: Recorded to tape in three days at a farmhouse above Venice, Allora is a chaotic, ecstatic record of hymnlike tenderness and full-band catharsis, made by Ben Seretan and his touring band mere weeks after the death of a close friend. It swings between grief and communal joy without settling on either.
lineage: Ben Seretan's prolific solo catalog (a 24-hour drone record, weekly song series) sits at the DIY, home-recording end of the indie-folk network.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Led by Chicago musician Chet Zenor, Lucky Cloud crafts dreamy, jazz-tinged indie rock full of rich textures: pedal steel, soft grooves and unorthodox melodies. Foreground is the project's debut full-length after growing from a solo bedroom project into a full band.
lineage: Part of the same Chicago Ruination Record Co. roster as Sima Cunningham, feeding into the city's twangy indie-folk scene.

album: Before You Turn Into a Dog
label: Self-released
description: Andy Weaver (drummer for Widowspeak, Castanets and his own band Wildflower) records intimate, handmade songs at home under the name Ruby of Thanks. Before You Turn Into a Dog values process over polish, preserving first-take performances of songs about love, work and finding peace.
lineage: Sits squarely in the Woodsist-orbit lo-fi home-recording tradition (Little Wings, John Andrews and the Yawns, Hand Habits), which itself descends from the DIY home-taping network.

label: Self-released
description: Hunter Park's project She Returns From War bills itself as "Cosmic Americana from South Carolina," and Ruthless leans into dance-pop elements alongside its country roots, cheekily needling Nashville conventions along the way.
lineage: A Southern songwriter reworking cosmic-country tropes with modern pop production, part of the same Southeastern DIY circuit as Minor Moon and V.V. Lightbody collaborators.

label: Polyvinyl
description: Ella O'Connor Williams's debut as Squirrel Flower is a hushed, unsettled record about drowning and being pulled under, quiet indie folk-rock that occasionally breaks into noise. It set the template for her louder, twangier records to come.
lineage: An early, quieter entry in an evolving catalog that grows steadily louder and more countrygaze-indebted with each release.

label: New Martian Records
description: Maine-born, Queens-based, The Clearwater Swimmers' self-titled debut flips between hushed intimacy and full electric-guitar surges, drawing direct comparisons to Neil Young's Harvest Moon and Jason Molina's Magnolia Electric Co.
lineage: Sits squarely in the Neil Young/Crazy Horse and Molina/Magnolia Electric Co. lineage that defines indie twang.

label: Woodsist
description: Morby's solo debut is a hushed, meandering set cut loose from Woods' bass-and-harmony pop, built on repeated guitar figures, mumbled Dylan-indebted phrasing, and a side-long title track that stretches past nine minutes. It set the template of unhurried, half-lit songwriting he'd refine for a decade.
lineage: Grew directly out of Morby's time as Woods' bassist and the Woodsist label scene, carrying that Crazy Horse/Velvets drone forward into his own solo run.

label: Woodsist
description: Morby's second solo LP tightens the songs from Harlem River into brisker, more country-inflected shapes, trading some of the drone for clearer verse-chorus structures and road-worn narrative detail. It's still recognizably Woodsist-scene lo-fi, but pointed toward the widescreen songwriting of his Dead Oceans records.
lineage: A bridge between Morby's Woods/Woodsist roots and the more polished, Dead Oceans-era songwriter he'd become on Singing Saw.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Morby's first album for Dead Oceans opens his sound way up: real string arrangements, a full band, and pedal steel behind an autobiographical suite about moving from New York to Los Angeles. The title track's looping, singing-saw hook is the clearest signal yet of his Laurel Canyon leanings.
lineage: Morby's turn from home-recorded folk toward orchestrated, Gram Parsons/Laurel Canyon-scaled songwriting, setting up City Music and the rest of his Dead Oceans run.
key_tracks: I Have Been to the Mountain

label: Dead Oceans
description: Conceived as Singing Saw's noisier city-set counterpart, City Music trades pastoral pedal steel for jangling electric guitars and a spoken-word title track that name-checks Lou Reed and Patti Smith. It's Morby's most explicitly Velvets/Modern Lovers-indebted record while still carrying his country-rock phrasing.
lineage: The urban mirror to Singing Saw's rural songs, pulling more directly from Morby's Velvet Underground and Jonathan Richman fandom.

label: Dead Oceans
description: A sprawling double-length song cycle about religion and mortality, built around piano, horns and gospel-adjacent backing vocals rather than guitar. It's Morby's most ambitious, least twangy record, but its questing, plainspoken spirituality keeps it in the Cosmic American Music lineage.
lineage: Extends Morby's widescreen Dead Oceans period into full song-cycle territory, echoing the loose spiritual searching of the Grateful Dead's American Beauty-era songwriting.

label: Woodsist
description: Denser and stranger than the debut, this record piles tape-collage noise interludes between fragile folk songs, sketching the push-pull between prettiness and racket that would define the band. Earl's warbling falsetto is already fully formed here.
lineage: Deepens the lo-fi Woodsist-scene template before the band's melodies sharpened on Songs of Shame.

label: Woodsist
description: Woods' sound had fully bloomed into warm, jammy classic-rock by this point, with the nine-minute title track stretching into extended guitar interplay reminiscent of the Dead and the Allmans. Earl's falsetto now floats over full-band arrangements rather than tape hiss.
lineage: Marks Woods' full transition from lo-fi folk to the jam-friendly cosmic country sound that runs through the rest of their catalog and the wider Woodsist scene.

album: City Sun Eater in the River of Light
label: Woodsist
description: Woods add horns and a looser, more percussive groove here, leaning into dub and Afrobeat-tinged rhythm sections under their usual searching guitar solos. It's the most rhythmically adventurous entry in a catalog otherwise built on jangle and drone.
lineage: Pushes the Woodsist-scene sound outward from straight cosmic-country jamming toward polyrhythmic, horn-inflected arrangements.

label: Woodsist
description: Written fast in the aftermath of the 2016 election, this is a quieter, more direct record than its predecessors, trading the horn-band sprawl for spare, plainspoken songs about grief and resolve. It's Woods at their most overtly political without losing the warm haze of their sound.
lineage: A stripped-back turn within the Woods catalog, closer in mood to their early folk records than the jam-heavy mid-2010s run.

label: Woodsist
description: Woods work in synths and drum machines alongside their usual guitar interplay here, giving the record a hazier, more nocturnal feel than their jam-band-leaning mid-2010s albums. It's still built on Earl's falsetto and the band's loping, Dead-adjacent chord changes.
lineage: Shows the Woodsist scene absorbing softer, synth-touched textures without losing its Crazy Horse/Dead backbone.

label: Woodsist
description: Woods' eleventh album returns to the warm, unhurried guitar-band sound of their mid-2010s peak, full of long fades and gently interlocking leads. Two decades in, it plays like a settled, confident restatement of everything the band and the Woodsist label have stood for.
lineage: A late-career synthesis of the whole Woods catalog, still rooted in Jeremy Earl's Woodsist label and the wider Brooklyn cosmic-country scene it helped launch.
key_tracks: Where Do You Go When You Dream

label: Brutal Honest
description: Williamson's second album on her own vanity label is sparser and more intimate than her later Mexican Summer records, built on fingerpicked guitar and a plainspoken alto working through heartbreak and searching. It's the clearest link between her early Texas-folk sound and the cosmic-country turn of Cosmic Wink.
lineage: A self-released bridge between Williamson's Native State debut and her Mexican Summer albums, still close to Texas singer-songwriter tradition.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: Gunn's first album to foreground his own singing over pure instrumental guitar playing, Time Off pairs raga-like fingerpicked figures with a laconic, half-sung drawl. It reads as the turning point where his American Primitive guitar background became actual songs.
lineage: Steve Gunn crosses over from the solo-guitar American Primitive lineage into full band-and-vocal cosmic country, a move he'd deepen on Way Out Weather.

label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: A full-band leap forward from Time Off, with a rhythm section giving Gunn's winding guitar lines somewhere to breathe and his voice settling into an easy, sun-warmed drawl. It's the record where critics started reaching for Television and the Dead in the same breath.
lineage: Consolidates Gunn's move from solo-guitar Primitivism into a proper cosmic-country band sound, setting up his run on Matador.

label: Matador
description: Gunn's Matador debut sharpens his songwriting into tighter, more rock-band arrangements while keeping the long instrumental release valves. Touring and travel are all over the lyrics, matching the record's road-worn, motorik-tinged guitar interplay.
lineage: First album for Matador Records, broadening Gunn's audience beyond the Paradise of Bachelors/Three Lobed underground while keeping the same guitar-forward songwriting.

label: Matador
description: A more melancholy, string-touched record made in the wake of his father's death, The Unseen in Between trades some of the road-song sprawl for tighter, more classically-structured songs. It's Gunn's most direct singer-songwriter statement to date.
lineage: Continues Gunn's Matador run with a turn toward orchestrated, personal songwriting rather than pure jam-length guitar pieces.

label: Matador
description: Recorded in France with a French rhythm section, Other You folds subtle synth textures into Gunn's guitar-first sound without losing its unhurried, sun-bleached feel. It plays like a hazier, more meditative sibling to Way Out Weather.
lineage: A late-period Matador record that keeps Gunn's cosmic-country songwriting intact while widening its palette with electronics.

label: Atlantic
description: A career-spanning live document assembled from years of shows, capturing how the band stretches its Dylan/Springsteen-via-Neil Young songs into extended, synth-lit jams on stage. It works as both a best-of and proof of the band's live reputation.
lineage: Distills a decade of The War on Drugs' Crazy Horse-meets-motorik guitar rock into its most expansive, jam-lengthened form.

label: Atlantic
description: A follow-up live set drawn from the I Don't Live Here Anymore tour, again showing how songs built in the studio around layered synths and guitar loops unfurl even longer on stage. Wild Pink's John Ross has singled out its version of 'Burning' as a highlight.
lineage: Second entry in the Live Drugs series, continuing the band's Crazy Horse/Dylan-descended arena-scale guitar rock in concert form.

label: Partisan Records
description: Burton's second album trades some of I Can Go With You's stark folk for fuller, Laurel Canyon-style arrangements, with pedal steel and strings framing his warm, unhurried baritone. It's gentler and more polished than the debut without losing its plainspoken sadness.
lineage: Moves Burton from the Tompkins Square country-folk revival roster toward a wider, Nashville-adjacent take on '70s soft country rock.

label: Human Error Music
description: Nashville pedal-steel sideman Spencer Cullum's debut as a bandleader is a sunny homage to '60s-'70s British and American folk-rock, cut with a rotating cast of Music City players like Erin Rae and Andrew Combs. It's less about his usual session role and more about letting his own songwriting lead.
lineage: Grows out of Cullum's work as a Nashville session pedal-steel player, channeling his English folk-rock upbringing through the city's cosmic-country underground.

label: Full Time Hobby
description: Cullum's second Coin Collection album pulls further from his English folk-rock reference points toward stranger, more subconscious songwriting, with guests like Rich Ruth and Caitlin Rose thickening the arrangements. It keeps the pedal-steel-led warmth while hiding its influences further from view.
lineage: A step deeper into Nashville's Coin Collection/Shrunken Elvis/Rich Ruth instrumentalist circle, still rooted in Cullum's pedal-steel session background.
key_tracks: What a Waste of an Echo

label: Domino
description: Released the same year as Wit's End as its looser, funnier counterpart, Humor Risk swaps that record's hush for jangling guitar-pop and McCombs' driest deadpan wit. It's one of his most purely enjoyable, least somber records.
lineage: The comic flip side to Wit's End within McCombs' prolific Domino years, closer to the Drag City deadpan-school tradition than his more mournful work.

label: Domino
description: A sprawling double album that runs from lean country-rock to hazier, longer jams, Big Wheel and Others is McCombs at his most expansive and least predictable. Its length and range make it feel like a summation of everything he'd tried across the previous decade.
lineage: A career-spanning-feeling double LP that pulls together McCombs' country-rock, folk and jam tendencies before his tighter ANTI- Records period.

label: Domino
description: Recorded largely in the Bay Area with early collaborators Jason Quever and Chris Cohen, Interior Live Oak returns to the more economical song structures of McCombs' earliest records while keeping his prime-era wit and melodic ease. It's a hopeful, clarifying record from an artist who's spent two decades circling extremes.
lineage: Closes a loop back to McCombs' Bay Area roots and Domino-era songwriting after years of ANTI- Records albums.
